q: Most musical instruments produce sound due to vibration of the string and air column.
e: The text explicitly states that most musical instruments produce sound due to the vibration of the string and air column.

q: Most musical instruments produce sound due to vibration of the solid body only.
e: Most musical instruments produce sound due to the vibration of the string and air column, not the solid body only.

q: These vibrations give rise to waves known as stationary waves in the string or air column.
e: The vibrations in musical instruments give rise to stationary waves in the string or air column.

q: These vibrations give rise to waves known as progressive waves in the string or air column.
e: The vibrations give rise to stationary waves in the string or air column, which then cause progressive waves to spread out.

q: Stationary waves cause progressive waves to spread out from a musical instrument.
e: The text states that stationary waves in the string or air column cause progressive waves to spread out from the musical instrument.

q: Waves are classified as progressive waves and stationary waves.
e: The textbook explicitly classifies waves into progressive waves and stationary waves in this context.

q: Progressive waves spread out from the region in which they are produced.
e: Progressive waves are defined as waves that spread out from the region in which they are produced.

q: Stationary waves spread out from the region in which they are produced.
e: Unlike progressive waves, stationary waves do not spread out but remain in the region in which they are produced.

q: Stationary waves are also called standing waves.
e: Because they remain in the region in which they are produced, stationary waves are also called standing waves.

q: Sound waves which travel in air when we speak are progressive waves.
e: The text gives sound waves traveling in air when we speak as an example of progressive waves.

q: Water waves which travel on the water surface when a stone is dropped are stationary waves.
e: Water waves which travel on the water surface when a stone is dropped are progressive waves, not stationary waves.

q: Progressive waves carry energy through the medium.
e: The text states that progressive waves carry energy through the medium.

q: The waves produced in hollow tubes such as flutes are stationary waves.
e: The waves produced in hollow tubes such as flutes and in string instruments are stationary waves.

q: The waves produced in string instruments such as violins and mandolins are progressive waves.
e: The waves produced in string instruments such as violins and mandolins are stationary waves.

q: A stationary wave is the resultant wave by the superposition of two waves of the same type having equal amplitudes and velocities traveling in opposite directions.
e: This is the exact definition of a stationary wave provided in the textbook.

q: A stationary wave is the resultant wave by the superposition of two waves of the same type having different amplitudes traveling in opposite directions.
e: A stationary wave is formed by the superposition of two waves having equal amplitudes and velocities traveling in opposite directions.

q: Waves have linearity property.
e: The textbook states that waves have a linearity property, which allows for the principle of superposition.

q: When two or more waves pass the same point, the resultant wave at that point is the sum of the individual waves.
e: This statement describes the principle of superposition.

q: If the resultant wave has a larger amplitude than that of individual waves, this is said to be destructive interference.
e: If the resultant wave has a larger amplitude than that of individual waves, this is said to be constructive interference.

q: If the resultant wave has a smaller amplitude than that of individual waves, this is said to be destructive interference.
e: Destructive interference occurs when the resultant wave has a smaller amplitude than the individual waves.

q: Nodes are produced at the locations where destructive interference occurs.
e: The hints in the reviewed exercise confirm that nodes are produced at locations where destructive interference occurs.

q: Antinodes are produced at the locations where constructive interference occurs.
e: The hints in the reviewed exercise confirm that antinodes are produced at locations where constructive interference occurs.

q: One characteristic of every stationary wave pattern is that there are points along the medium, which are called nodes and antinodes.
e: This is a stated characteristic of every stationary wave pattern.

q: The points marked N are always moving with maximum amplitude.
e: The points marked N are always stationary and are called nodes.

q: The points between nodes are vibrating with different amplitudes.
e: The text states that the points between nodes vibrate with different amplitudes.

q: The mid-points between successive nodes have the largest amplitudes and are called antinodes.
e: Antinodes are defined as the mid-points between successive nodes, which have the largest amplitudes.

q: Nodes and antinodes always alternate and are equally spaced.
e: The textbook explicitly states that nodes and antinodes always alternate and are equally spaced.

q: The distance between two successive nodes is equal to $\lambda$ where $\lambda$ is the wavelength.
e: The distance between two successive nodes (or antinodes) is equal to $\lambda/2$, not $\lambda$.

q: The distance between two successive nodes (or) antinodes is equal to $\lambda/2$ where $\lambda$ is the wavelength.
e: The textbook states that the distance between two successive nodes or antinodes is $\lambda/2$.

q: The distance from a node to the nearest antinode is equal to $\lambda/4$.
e: The distance from a node to the nearest antinode is exactly one-quarter of the wavelength ($\lambda/4$).

q: In most of the musical instruments, the stretched strings act as a source of sound.
e: The text states that in most musical instruments like violins and mandolins, stretched strings act as a source of sound.

q: When the stretched strings are plucked, progressive waves are produced.
e: When the stretched strings are plucked, stationary waves are produced, not progressive waves.

q: When the string is plucked, the stationary waves with nodes at the fixed ends are formed.
e: The fixed ends of a plucked string cannot move, so nodes are formed at these ends.

q: When the string is plucked, the stationary waves with antinodes at the fixed ends are formed.
e: Stationary waves formed on a string rigidly fixed at both ends have nodes, not antinodes, at the fixed ends.

q: The waves that are formed on the string are called harmonics.
e: The specific frequencies and wave patterns formed on the plucked string are called harmonics.

q: For the $n^{th}$ harmonic, the wavelength is given by $\lambda_n = rac{2l}{n}$ where $n=1, 2, 3, ...$.
e: This is the correct formula for the wavelength of the $n^{th}$ harmonic of a vibrating string of length $l$.

q: For the $n^{th}$ harmonic, the wavelength is given by $\lambda_n = rac{l}{n}$ where $n=1, 2, 3, ...$.
e: The correct formula for the wavelength of the $n^{th}$ harmonic is $\lambda_n =  rac{2l}{n}$, not $ rac{l}{n}$.

q: The corresponding frequencies are calculated from $v = f_n \lambda_n$, where $v$ is the velocity of the wave in a string.
e: The wave equation $v = f_n \lambda_n$ is used to calculate the corresponding frequencies.

q: The frequencies of a vibrating string of length $l$ are given by $f_n = rac{nv}{2l}$ where $n=1, 2, 3, ...$.
e: This is the correct formula for the frequencies of a vibrating string of length $l$.

q: Vibration of a string in one single segment is called the fundamental or first harmonic.
e: The text defines the vibration of a string in one single segment as the fundamental or first harmonic.

q: Vibration of a string in one single segment is called the first overtone.
e: Vibration of a string in one single segment is called the fundamental or first harmonic, not the first overtone.

q: A musical tone which is part of the harmonic series above a fundamental note is called an overtone.
e: The textbook defines an overtone as a musical tone which is part of the harmonic series above a fundamental note.

q: The velocity of a wave in a vibrating string depends on the tension of the string and mass per unit length of the string.
e: The velocity of a wave in a vibrating string is determined by the tension and the mass per unit length.

q: The velocity of a wave in a vibrating string is given by the formula $v = \sqrt{ rac{T}{\mu}}$.
e: This is the correct formula relating wave velocity to tension $T$ and mass per unit length $\mu$.

q: The velocity of a wave in a vibrating string is given by the formula $v = \sqrt{ rac{\mu}{T}}$.
e: The correct formula is $v = \sqrt{ rac{T}{\mu}}$, not $\sqrt{ rac{\mu}{T}}$.

q: In the formula $v = \sqrt{ rac{T}{\mu}}$, $T$ represents the tension of the string.
e: $T$ is explicitly defined as the tension of the string in the textbook.

q: In the formula $v = \sqrt{ rac{T}{\mu}}$, $\mu$ represents the total mass of the string.
e: $\mu$ represents the mass per unit length of the string, not the total mass.

q: The frequencies of the vibrating string can also be written in terms of $T$ and $\mu$ as $f_n = rac{n}{2l} \sqrt{ rac{T}{\mu}}$.
e: Substituting the velocity formula into the frequency formula yields this correct expression.

q: For the second harmonic, $n=2$, the frequency is $f_2 = 2f_1$.
e: The second harmonic has twice the frequency of the first harmonic (fundamental frequency).

q: For the third harmonic, $n=3$, the frequency is $f_3 = 3f_1$.
e: The third harmonic has three times the frequency of the first harmonic.

q: Mass per unit length of the string is the ratio of mass to length of the string.
e: This is the definition of mass per unit length, represented as $\mu =  rac{m}{l}$.

q: Mass per unit length can be expressed as $\mu = ho A$, where $A$ is the uniform cross-sectional area of the string.
e: Since $m = ho V = ho A l$, dividing by $l$ gives $\mu = ho A$.

q: In the expression $\mu = ho A$, $ ho$ represents the volume of the string.
e: In the expression $\mu = ho A$, $ho$ represents the density of the material of the string, not the volume.

q: If one of the pendulums is set up into oscillation, the others will begin to oscillate because they are coupled by vibrations in a flexible beam.
e: The text explains that pendulums suspended from a flexible beam are coupled by vibrations in the beam.

q: Pendulum C, whose length is the same as that of A, will oscillate with the greatest amplitude since its natural frequency matches that of pendulum A.
e: Matching natural frequencies lead to maximum amplitude oscillation, which is the condition for resonance.

q: The amplitude of the motion reaches a maximum when the frequency of the driving force equals the natural frequency of the system.
e: This is the defining condition for resonance as stated in the textbook.

q: Under the condition of maximum amplitude, the system is said to be in resonance.
e: When the driving frequency equals the natural frequency, the system is in resonance.

q: Natural frequency is the frequency at which a system tends to oscillate in the presence of any driving force.
e: Natural frequency is the frequency at which a system tends to oscillate in the absence of any driving force.

q: Natural frequency is the frequency at which a system tends to oscillate in the absence of any driving force.
e: This is the exact definition of natural frequency provided in the text.

q: If a vibrating tuning fork is placed over the open end of a glass tube partly filled with water, the sound of the tuning fork can be greatly amplified under certain conditions.
e: This describes the resonance column experiment where amplification occurs at specific air column lengths.

q: The length of the air column in the resonance tube can be varied by raising or lowering the water level.
e: Adjusting the water level changes the length of the air column to find resonance points.

q: The wave is sent down the air column in the tube and it is reflected upwards when it hits the water surface.
e: The water surface acts as a closed end, reflecting the wave upwards.

q: The resonance tube will have an antinode near the open end and a node at the water surface.
e: Air molecules can move freely at the open end (antinode) but cannot move at the water surface (node).

q: The water at the closed end will not allow the air molecules to move downward, so an antinode will be formed.
e: Because the air molecules cannot move at the water surface, a node is formed, not an antinode.

q: Resonance can only be produced under the situation where a node is formed at the water surface and an antinode is formed at the open end.
e: This boundary condition is necessary for resonance in a closed-end air column.

q: Since the antinodes lie just beyond the end of the tube, a correction $c$ is added to the length of the air column.
e: End correction $c$ accounts for the fact that the antinode is slightly outside the physical open end of the tube.

q: For the first resonance, the length of the air column is given by $l_1 + c = rac{\lambda}{4}$.
e: The first resonance occurs when the effective length of the air column is one-quarter of the wavelength.

q: For the second resonance, the length of the air column is given by $l_2 + c = rac{3\lambda}{4}$.
e: The second resonance occurs when the effective length of the air column is three-quarters of the wavelength.

q: Using the resonance equations, the wavelength of the vibrating air column is $\lambda = 2(l_2 - l_1)$.
e: Subtracting the first resonance equation from the second eliminates $c$ and yields $\lambda = 2(l_2 - l_1)$.

q: At resonance, the frequency $f$ of the tuning fork is equal to the frequency of the vibrating air column.
e: Resonance occurs when the driving frequency (tuning fork) matches the natural frequency of the air column.

q: The velocity of sound can be found using the formula $v = f\lambda$.
e: Once the wavelength is determined from resonance lengths, the velocity of sound is calculated using $v = f\lambda$.

q: In a closed organ pipe, one end is opened and another end is closed.
e: This is the defining structural characteristic of a closed organ pipe.

q: A whistle is an example of an open organ pipe.
e: A whistle is given as an example of a closed organ pipe, not an open organ pipe.

q: In closed organ pipes, an antinode exists near the open end while a node is formed at the closed end.
e: This matches the boundary conditions for a closed organ pipe.

q: The wavelength of the $n^{th}$ harmonic for a vibrating air column in a closed organ pipe is $\lambda_n = rac{4l}{n}$ where $n=1, 3, 5, ...$.
e: This is the correct formula for the wavelengths of harmonics in a closed organ pipe.

q: The wavelength of the $n^{th}$ harmonic for a vibrating air column in a closed organ pipe is $\lambda_n = rac{2l}{n}$ where $n=1, 2, 3, ...$.
e: The formula $\lambda_n =  rac{2l}{n}$ applies to open organ pipes, not closed organ pipes.

q: The frequency of a closed organ pipe is given by $f_n = rac{nv}{4l}$ where $n=1, 3, 5, ...$.
e: This is the correct formula for the resonant frequencies of a closed organ pipe.

q: A closed organ pipe produces both odd and even harmonics.
e: A closed organ pipe produces only odd harmonics ($n=1, 3, 5, ...$).

q: In a closed organ pipe, the third harmonic is called the first overtone.
e: Since even harmonics are missing, the next harmonic after the fundamental ($n=1$) is the third harmonic ($n=3$), which is the first overtone.

q: In a closed organ pipe, the fifth harmonic is called the second overtone.
e: Following the fundamental and first overtone, the fifth harmonic ($n=5$) is the second overtone.

q: The stationary wave with a single node in the open organ pipe corresponds to the fundamental frequency (first harmonic).
e: In an open organ pipe, the fundamental frequency has a single node in the middle and antinodes at both ends.

q: In an open organ pipe, the stationary wave with two nodes is the second harmonic (or) first overtone.
e: The text states that the stationary wave with two nodes in an open organ pipe corresponds to the second harmonic or first overtone.

q: A flute is an example of an open organ pipe.
e: The textbook explicitly identifies a flute as an open organ pipe.

q: A clarinet can be modeled as a pipe closed at one end.
e: The text states that a clarinet can be modeled as a pipe closed at one end.

q: The wavelength for the $n^{th}$ harmonic in an open organ pipe is $\lambda_n = rac{2l}{n}$ where $n=1, 2, 3, ...$.
e: This is the correct formula for the wavelengths of harmonics in an open organ pipe.

q: The frequencies of a vibrating air column in an open organ pipe are $f_n = rac{nv}{2l}$ where $n=1, 2, 3, ...$.
e: This is the correct formula for the resonant frequencies of an open organ pipe.

q: Beats are the periodic fluctuation heard in the intensity of sound when two sound waves of slightly different frequencies interfere with one another.
e: This is the exact definition of beats provided in the textbook.

q: The number of beats per second is the sum of the frequencies of the two sources.
e: The number of beats per second (beat frequency) is the difference in frequency between the two sources, not the sum.

q: The beat frequency is given by the formula $f_b = |f_1 - f_2|$.
e: The beat frequency is the absolute difference between the frequencies of the two interfering sound sources.

q: The intensity of a wave is the power or energy per unit time transported per unit cross-sectional area.
e: This is the exact definition of wave intensity provided in the textbook.

q: The intensity of a wave is the power transported per unit volume.
e: Intensity is power transported per unit cross-sectional area, not per unit volume.

q: The formula for the intensity of a wave is $I = rac{P}{A}$.
e: Intensity $I$ is defined as power $P$ divided by cross-sectional area $A$.

q: In SI units, the unit of intensity of a wave is watt per metre squared ($W m^{-2}$).
e: The textbook explicitly states that the SI unit for wave intensity is $W m^{-2}$.

q: If the air around the source is perfectly uniform, the sound power propagated in all directions is the same.
e: In a perfectly uniform medium, sound propagates isotropically (equally in all directions).

q: In a perfectly uniform medium, the propagated sound wave is represented by a plane wave.
e: In a perfectly uniform medium, the propagated sound wave from a point source is represented by a spherical wave.

q: By considering the source of sound as a point source, the sound wave can be distributed uniformly over a spherical wave front of area $4\pi r^2$.
e: The surface area of a sphere of radius $r$ is $4\pi r^2$, over which the sound power is distributed.

q: The wave intensity at a distance $r$ from a point source is given by $I = rac{P}{4\pi r^2}$.
e: This formula correctly applies the definition of intensity to a spherical wave front.

q: For a particular source, intensity varies directly with the square of the distance from the source.
e: For a particular source, intensity varies inversely with the square of the distance from the source.

q: For a particular source, intensity varies inversely with the square of the distance from the source.
e: This relationship is known as the inverse square law for wave intensity.

q: Intensity of a wave obeys the inverse square law.
e: The textbook explicitly states that the intensity of a wave obeys the inverse square law.

q: The intensity of a wave is directly proportional to the square of the amplitude of the wave.
e: The text states that wave intensity is directly proportional to the square of its amplitude.

q: The intensity of a wave is directly proportional to the amplitude of the wave.
e: The intensity of a wave is directly proportional to the square of the amplitude, not the amplitude itself.

q: Sound level is expressed in decibel (dB).
e: The decibel (dB) is the unit used to express sound level.

q: Sound with very high intensities can be harmful to human ears.
e: The text warns that sound with very high intensities can be harmful.

q: Sound levels of 140 to 150 dB can rupture eardrums and cause permanent hearing loss.
e: The textbook explicitly states that sound levels in this range can rupture eardrums and cause permanent hearing loss.

q: Sound levels of 140 to 150 dB can cause only temporary hearing loss.
e: Sound levels of 140 to 150 dB can cause permanent hearing loss, not just temporary.

q: Longer exposure to lower sound (noise) levels can also cause hearing damage.
e: The text notes that prolonged exposure to lower noise levels is also harmful.

q: According to the permissible noise exposure limits, the maximum duration per day for a sound level of 90 dB is 8 hours.
e: Table 6.1 lists 8 hours as the maximum duration per day for a 90 dB sound level.

q: According to the permissible noise exposure limits, the maximum duration per day for a sound level of 95 dB is 4 hours.
e: Table 6.1 lists 4 hours as the maximum duration per day for a 95 dB sound level.

q: According to the permissible noise exposure limits, the maximum duration per day for a sound level of 100 dB is 2 hours.
e: Table 6.1 lists 2 hours as the maximum duration per day for a 100 dB sound level.

q: According to the permissible noise exposure limits, the maximum duration per day for a sound level of 105 dB is 1 hour.
e: Table 6.1 lists 1 hour as the maximum duration per day for a 105 dB sound level.
